source.title: An Inertial Newton Algorithm for Deep Learning
source.authors: Camille Castera; J. Bolte; C. Févotte; Edouard Pauwels

record.tranche_reason: Compares optimizer methods on image-classification test accuracy, using a different optimizer and task setup from V4.
record.gate_note: The optimizer comparisons bear on V4. Other optimizer results and theoretical convergence claims do not measure the training–test gap. Figure 3 reports training loss and test accuracy curves; the text does not give exact test-accuracy values or describe Adam's test accuracy relative to SGD.
record.test_reason: Figure 3 directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD using held-out image-classification accuracy under limited learning-rate tuning, the method and measure relevant to V4. The supplied text does not preserve the plotted curves well enough to determine their relative test accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the empirical conclusion: INNA is competitive with established optimizers, INNA and Adam outperform SGD and Adagrad in training, and INNA usually achieves the best test accuracy, especially on CIFAR-100. The paper also emphasizes INNA's convergence guarantees and flexibility under limited tuning. It does not explicitly conclude that Adam generalizes worse than SGD.
record.recipe_differences: Tests a new inertial Newton optimizer against SGD, ADAGRAD and ADAM on NiN image classifiers; uses a grid search for initial step size and five random initializations.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset changes the reported comparison; the text highlights CIFAR-100 as a setting where INNA especially achieves the best accuracy. Step-size decay also changes INNA's relative training performance, but this is not a V4 test result.

fits_no_version.finding: INNA and Adam optimize training loss better than SGD and Adagrad; changing INNA's step-size decay can further accelerate training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice and step-size decay affect training efficiency; these results alone do not determine held-out generalization.

record.problems: The paper does not provide exact test-accuracy values in text for the optimizer comparisons; plotted lines and ranges are the evidence. The text does not report Adam's test accuracy relative to SGD.
record.rows_left_out: No additional optimizer comparison rows were extracted from Figure 3; the non-Adam method curves do not add evidence about V4 beyond the listed comparisons. Figure 4 compares INNA step-size schedules with ADAM but concerns training loss and optimizer speed, not held-out performance.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out comparisons.
Width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language-model exceptions.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations to large-batch training.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No directional verdict is justified from the supplied figure text. Initial learning rates were selected by training loss after 15 epochs, without test-data tuning; comparisons extend to 200 epochs over five initializations. Adagrad versus SGD also bears on V4, but its omitted rows are explicitly declared in rows_left_out and its curve ordering is likewise unreadable here. INNA's superiority alone does not settle V4.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Language benchmarks, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language models.
